entities.name: Menelaus of Alexandria
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Menelaus of Alexandria, a pivotal Greek mathematician and astronomer active around 100 CE, was a central figure in the intellectual efflorescence of Roman Egypt. Operating from Alexandria, a preeminent center of Hellenistic learning, he profoundly influenced the development of spherical geometry and trigonometry. His magnum opus, *Sphaerica*, laid foundational principles for celestial mechanics and navigation, establishing him as a crucial link between Euclidean geometry and the advanced astronomical calculations of subsequent eras. He is widely credited with the formulation of Menelaus's theorem and pioneering the concept of geodesics on curved surfaces.

His primary contribution, *Sphaerica*, originally written in three books, is preserved largely through an Arabic translation by Ishaq ibn Hunayn from the 9th century, subsequently translated into Latin. In this seminal work, Menelaus systematically extended the principles of Euclidean plane geometry to spherical surfaces. He notably proved what became known as Menelaus's theorem (or the 'rule of six quantities'), a fundamental relationship between the angles and arc lengths of a spherical triangle intersected by a transversal arc. His astronomical observations, including a lunar occultation recorded in 98 CE in Rome, provided empirical data later incorporated by Claudius Ptolemy in the *Almagest*.
